claim: Cerebellar granule cells (GCs) make up the majority of all neurons in the vertebrate brain.
source: Cerebellar granule cells (GCs) make up the majority of all neurons in the vertebrate brain, but heterogeneities among GCs and potential functional consequences are poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement presented in the abstract as established fact about GC abundance in the vertebrate brain.

claim: GCs closer to the white matter (inner-zone GCs) had higher firing thresholds than GCs closer to the Purkinje cell layer (outer-zone GCs).
source: GCs closer to the white matter (inner-zone GCs) had higher firing thresholds and could sustain firing with larger current inputs than GCs closer to the Purkinje cell layer (outer-zone GCs).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1E showing current threshold measurements.

claim: Inner-zone GCs could sustain firing with larger current inputs than outer-zone GCs.
source: GCs closer to the white matter (inner-zone GCs) had higher firing thresholds and could sustain firing with larger current inputs than GCs closer to the Purkinje cell layer (outer-zone GCs).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1F showing the current needed to achieve maximum firing rate.

claim: Inner- and outer-zone GCs preferentially respond to high- and low-frequency mossy fiber inputs, respectively.
source: Dynamic Clamp experiments showed that inner- and outer-zone GCs preferentially respond to high- and low-frequency mossy fiber inputs, respectively, enabling dispersion of the mossy fiber input into its frequency components as performed by a Fourier transformation.
evidence: This is supported by Dynamic Clamp experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The biophysical gradients enable dispersion of the mossy fiber input into its frequency components as performed by a Fourier transformation.
source: Dynamic Clamp experiments showed that inner- and outer-zone GCs preferentially respond to high- and low-frequency mossy fiber inputs, respectively, enabling dispersion of the mossy fiber input into its frequency components as performed by a Fourier transformation.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data from Dynamic Clamp experiments and represents an inference about the functional consequence.

claim: Inner-zone GCs have faster axonal conduction velocity than outer-zone GCs.
source: Furthermore, inner-zone GCs have faster axonal conduction velocity and elicit faster synaptic potentials in Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements of compound action potentials shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Inner-zone GCs elicit faster synaptic potentials in Purkinje cells than outer-zone GCs.
source: Furthermore, inner-zone GCs have faster axonal conduction velocity and elicit faster synaptic potentials in Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on EPSP kinetics in PCs shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The biophysical gradients improve spike-timing precision of Purkinje cells.
source: Neuronal network modeling revealed that these gradients improve spike-timing precision of Purkinje cells and decrease the number of GCs required to learn spike-sequences.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 8.

claim: The biophysical gradients decrease the number of GCs required to learn spike-sequences.
source: Neuronal network modeling revealed that these gradients improve spike-timing precision of Purkinje cells and decrease the number of GCs required to learn spike-sequences.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Digital audio compression (e.g. 'MP3') relies on Fourier transformations.
source: Digital audio compression (e.g. 'MP3'; Jayant et al., 1993) and image compression (e.g. 'JPEG'; Wallace, 1992) rely on Fourier transformations, which decompose a signal (e.g. sound amplitude as a function of time or image intensity as a function of space) into its frequency components (power as a function of frequency).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on digital compression.

claim: Image compression (e.g. 'JPEG') relies on Fourier transformations.
source: Digital audio compression (e.g. 'MP3'; Jayant et al., 1993) and image compression (e.g. 'JPEG'; Wallace, 1992) rely on Fourier transformations, which decompose a signal (e.g. sound amplitude as a function of time or image intensity as a function of space) into its frequency components (power as a function of frequency).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on digital compression.

claim: Fourier transformations decompose a signal into its frequency components.
source: Digital audio compression (e.g. 'MP3'; Jayant et al., 1993) and image compression (e.g. 'JPEG'; Wallace, 1992) rely on Fourier transformations, which decompose a signal (e.g. sound amplitude as a function of time or image intensity as a function of space) into its frequency components (power as a function of frequency).
evidence: This is established mathematical knowledge about Fourier transformations.

claim: Pyramidal neurons in the visual cortex are tuned to different inputs or different input strengths.
source: Interestingly, there are indications that for example pyramidal neurons in the visual cortex and in the hippocampus are tuned to different inputs or different input strengths (Cembrowski and Spruston, 2019; Fletcher and Williams, 2019; Soltesz and Losonczy, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Pyramidal neurons in the hippocampus are tuned to different inputs or different input strengths.
source: Interestingly, there are indications that for example pyramidal neurons in the visual cortex and in the hippocampus are tuned to different inputs or different input strengths (Cembrowski and Spruston, 2019; Fletcher and Williams, 2019; Soltesz and Losonczy, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The firing frequency of Purkinje cells is closely related to movement.
source: In the cerebellum, the firing frequency of Purkinje cells (PCs) (Heiney et al., 2014; Herzfeld et al., 2015; Hewitt et al., 2011; Medina and Lisberger, 2007; Payne et al., 2019; Sarnaik and Raman, 2018; Witter et al., 2013) or the timing of spikes (Brown and Raman, 2018; Sarnaik and Raman, 2018) have been shown to be closely related to movement.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The timing of spikes in Purkinje cells is closely related to movement.
source: In the cerebellum, the firing frequency of Purkinje cells (PCs) (Heiney et al., 2014; Herzfeld et al., 2015; Hewitt et al., 2011; Medina and Lisberger, 2007; Payne et al., 2019; Sarnaik and Raman, 2018; Witter et al., 2013) or the timing of spikes (Brown and Raman, 2018; Sarnaik and Raman, 2018) have been shown to be closely related to movement.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cerebellar pathology impairs precision in motor learning tasks.
source: Indeed, cerebellar pathology impairs precision in motor learning tasks (Gibo et al., 2013; Martin et al., 1996) and timing of rhythmic learning tasks (Keele and Ivry, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cerebellar pathology impairs timing of rhythmic learning tasks.
source: Indeed, cerebellar pathology impairs precision in motor learning tasks (Gibo et al., 2013; Martin et al., 1996) and timing of rhythmic learning tasks (Keele and Ivry, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inputs from mossy fibers are processed by GCs and transmitted via their parallel fiber axons to PCs.
source: Inputs from mossy fibers (MFs) are processed by GCs and transmitted via their parallel fiber (PF) axons to PCs, which provide the sole output from the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar circuit architecture.

claim: Purkinje cells provide the sole output from the cerebellar cortex.
source: Inputs from mossy fibers (MFs) are processed by GCs and transmitted via their parallel fiber (PF) axons to PCs, which provide the sole output from the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar circuit architecture.

claim: GCs provide pattern separation and conversion of the MF input into a sparser representation.
source: GCs represent the first stage in cerebellar processing and have been proposed to provide pattern separation and conversion of the MF input into a sparser representation (recently reviewed by Cayco-Gajic and Silver, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Mossy fiber inputs show a wide variety of signaling frequencies, ranging from slow modulating activity to kilohertz bursts of activity.
source: These MF inputs show a wide variety of signaling frequencies, ranging from slow modulating activity to kilohertz bursts of activity (Arenz et al., 2008; Rancz et al., 2007; Ritzau-Jost et al., 2014; van Kan et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inner-zone GCs were less excitable compared with outer-zone GCs upon current injection.
source: Upon current injection, inner-zone GCs were less excitable compared with outer-zone GCs (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Inner-zone GCs needed higher current injections to fire an action potential (56.8 ± 2.6 pA) compared with outer-zone GCs (39.4 ± 2.0 pA).
source: inner-zone GCs needed higher current injections to fire an action potential (inner: 56.8 ± 2.6 pA vs. middle: 51.2 ± 2.0 pA vs. outer: 39.4 ± 2.0 pA; n = 38, 25, and 37, respectively; PKruskal-Wallis <0.0001; Figure 1E)
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements with statistical significance testing.

claim: Inner-zone GCs needed higher current injections to achieve the maximum firing rate (224.6 ± 9.8 pA) compared with outer-zone GCs (174.3 ± 9.0 pA).
source: inner-zone GCs needed higher current injections to fire an action potential (inner: 56.8 ± 2.6 pA vs. middle: 51.2 ± 2.0 pA vs. outer: 39.4 ± 2.0 pA; n = 38, 25, and 37, respectively; PKruskal-Wallis <0.0001; Figure 1E) and to achieve the maximum firing rate compared with middle- and outer-zone GCs (inner: 224.6 ± 9.8 pA vs. middle: 190.8 ± 9.6 pA vs. outer: 174.3 ± 9.0 pA, respectively; PKruskal-Wallis = 0.002; Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements with statistical significance testing.

claim: Inner-zone GCs had a more depolarized threshold for action potential generation (−38.0 ± 0.7 mV) compared with outer-zone GCs (−41.4 ± 0.6 mV).
source: Consistently, inner-zone GCs had a more depolarized threshold for action potential generation compared with middle- and outer-zone GCs (−38.0 ± 0.7 mV vs. −38.2 ± 0.8 mV vs. −41.4 ± 0.6 mV; PKruskal-Wallis = 0.003; Figure 1G)
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements with statistical significance testing.

claim: Inner-zone GCs had a lower input resistance (486 ± 27 MΩ) compared with outer-zone GCs (791 ± 63 MΩ).
source: inner-zone GCs had a more depolarized threshold for action potential generation compared with middle- and outer-zone GCs (−38.0 ± 0.7 mV vs. −38.2 ± 0.8 mV vs. −41.4 ± 0.6 mV; PKruskal-Wallis = 0.003; Figure 1G) and a lower input resistance (486 ± 27 MΩ vs. 494 ± 27 MΩ vs. 791 ± 63 MΩ; PKruskal-Wallis = <0.0001; Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements with statistical significance testing.

claim: The capacitance of inner-zone GCs (5.8 ± 0.2 pF) was significantly larger compared with outer-zone GCs (4.6 ± 0.1 pF).
source: Furthermore, the capacitance of inner-zone GCs was significantly larger compared with outer-zone GCs (inner: 5.8 ± 0.2 pF vs. middle: 5.8 ± 0.2 pF vs. outer: 4.6 ± 0.1 pF; PKruskal-Wallis = <0.0001 Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements with statistical significance testing.

claim: Depolarization block occurred in inner-zone GCs at higher current inputs than for outer-zone GCs.
source: In agreement with these findings, we observed depolarization block in inner-zone GCs at higher current inputs than for outer-zone GCs (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: A larger delay of the first spike was observed in inner- compared with outer-zone GCs.
source: Furthermore, a larger delay of the first spike was observed in inner- compared with outer-zone GCs (Figure 1J; PKruskal-Wallis = 0.0001; Figure 1K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements with statistical significance testing.

claim: The delay with 60 pA current injection was 48 ± 6 ms for inner-zone GCs and 23 ± 2 ms for outer-zone GCs.
source: The delay with 60 pA current injection was 48 ± 6 ms for inner-, 38 ± 4 ms for middle-, and 23 ± 2 ms for outer-zone GCs (n = 32, 25, and 37, respectively; note that 6 out of 38 inner-zone GCs did not fire an action potential at 60 pA).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements.

claim: The action potential half-width of inner-zone GCs (122 ± 2 µs) was significantly shorter than outer-zone GCs (143 ± 4 µs).
source: Finally, the action potential half-width of GCs differed significantly between the three zones (inner: 122 ± 2 µs vs. middle: 137 ± 4 µs vs. outer: 143 ± 4 µs; PKruskal-Wallis = 0.0001; Figure 1L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements with statistical significance testing.

claim: The maximum Kv current at -60 mV was significantly higher in inner-zone GCs (282 ± 29 pA) compared with outer-zone GCs (221 ± 28 pA).
source: The maximum Kv current at -60 mV was significantly higher in inner-zone GCs (282 ± 29 pA, n = 48) compared with outer-zone GCs (221 ± 28 pA, n = 54, PMann-Whitney = 0.04; Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements with statistical significance testing.

claim: The steady-state activation curve of Kv channels was not different between inner- and outer-zone GCs.
source: Neither the steady-state activation curve (Figure 2C) nor the degree of inactivation (Figure 2D) was different between the two GC populations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The degree of inactivation of Kv channels was not different between inner- and outer-zone GCs.
source: Neither the steady-state activation curve (Figure 2C) nor the degree of inactivation (Figure 2D) was different between the two GC populations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Steady-state inactivation of Kv channels was similar between inner- and outer-zone GCs.
source: Furthermore, steady-state inactivation, which was investigated with different holding potentials, was similar between inner- and outer-zone GCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Inner- and outer-zone GCs have a similar composition of Kv channels, but inner-zone GCs have a higher Kv channel density.
source: These data suggest that inner- and outer-zone GCs have a similar composition of Kv channels, but inner-zone GCs have a higher Kv channel density.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing similar kinetics but different maximum currents.

claim: The larger Kv currents in inner-zone GCs are consistent with the short action potential duration of inner-zone GCs.
source: The larger Kv currents in inner-zone GCs are consistent with the short action potential duration of inner-zone GCs (cf. Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the Kv current data to the action potential duration data.

claim: There were no significant differences in the amplitude or kinetics of EPSCs in inner- and outer-zone GCs after single MF stimulation.
source: We found no significant differences in the amplitude or kinetics of EPSCs in inner- and outer-zone GCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: At a holding potential of −70 mV, inner-zone GCs responded preferentially to high-frequency MF inputs up to 300 Hz.
source: At a holding potential of −70 mV, commonly occurring in vivo (Chadderton et al., 2004), inner-zone GCs responded preferentially to high-frequency MF inputs up to 300 Hz, while outer-zone GCs responded preferentially to low-frequency inputs up to 100 Hz (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Dynamic Clamp experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: At a holding potential of −70 mV, outer-zone GCs responded preferentially to low-frequency MF inputs up to 100 Hz.
source: At a holding potential of −70 mV, commonly occurring in vivo (Chadderton et al., 2004), inner-zone GCs responded preferentially to high-frequency MF inputs up to 300 Hz, while outer-zone GCs responded preferentially to low-frequency inputs up to 100 Hz (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Dynamic Clamp experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The mean phase angle at which inner-zone GCs preferentially fired was 162 ± 8°, representing an average firing frequency of 284 Hz.
source: The mean phase angle, at which GC preferentially fired, was 162 ± 8° for inner-zone (n = 10) and 100 ± 20° for outer-zone GCs (n = 7; PMann-Whitney = 0.02; Figure 4C), representing an average firing frequency of 284 and 116 Hz for inner- and outer-zone GCs, respectively (cf. Equation 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements with statistical significance testing.

claim: The mean phase angle at which outer-zone GCs preferentially fired was 100 ± 20°, representing an average firing frequency of 116 Hz.
source: The mean phase angle, at which GC preferentially fired, was 162 ± 8° for inner-zone (n = 10) and 100 ± 20° for outer-zone GCs (n = 7; PMann-Whitney = 0.02; Figure 4C), representing an average firing frequency of 284 and 116 Hz for inner- and outer-zone GCs, respectively (cf. Equation 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements with statistical significance testing.

claim: The length of the ascending GC axon showed considerable variation (196 ± 5.5 μm, range: 144 to 291 μm).
source: Even though the length of the ascending GC axon showed considerable variation (196 ± 5.5 μm, range: 144 to 291 μm, n = 39 axons in n = 6 mice), after normalization for the thickness of the molecular and GC layers, the GC soma position was significantly correlated with the position of the bifurcation in the GC axon (Figure 5C,D; R = –0.86, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements from DiI labeling experiments.

claim: The GC soma position was significantly correlated with the position of the bifurcation in the GC axon (R = –0.86, p<0.001).
source: Even though the length of the ascending GC axon showed considerable variation (196 ± 5.5 μm, range: 144 to 291 μm, n = 39 axons in n = 6 mice), after normalization for the thickness of the molecular and GC layers, the GC soma position was significantly correlated with the position of the bifurcation in the GC axon (Figure 5C,D; R = –0.86, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements with statistical significance testing.

claim: Inner-zone GCs preferentially give rise to PF located near the PC layer.
source: These data show that inner-zone GCs preferentially give rise to PF located near the PC layer (inner-zone PFs) and outer-zone GC give rise to PF near the surface of the cerebellar cortex (outer-zone PFs).
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Outer-zone GCs give rise to PF near the surface of the cerebellar cortex.
source: These data show that inner-zone GCs preferentially give rise to PF located near the PC layer (inner-zone PFs) and outer-zone GC give rise to PF near the surface of the cerebellar cortex (outer-zone PFs).
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Inner-zone PFs have significantly larger diameters (182 ± 2.6 nm) compared with outer-zone PFs (145 ± 1.7 nm).
source: First, we compared the PF diameters in electron microscopic images of parasagittal sections of lobule V of mouse cerebellum and found significantly larger diameters for inner-zone PFs compared with middle- and outer-zone PFs (182 ± 2.6 nm, n = 703 vs. 159 ± 2.0 nm, n = 819 vs. 145 ± 1.7 nm, n = 1024 Figure 6A–C; PKruskal-Wallis <0.0001)
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy measurements with statistical significance testing.

claim: The gradient in PF diameter is in agreement with previous investigations reported in cat, monkey, rat, and mouse.
source: First, we compared the PF diameters in electron microscopic images of parasagittal sections of lobule V of mouse cerebellum and found significantly larger diameters for inner-zone PFs compared with middle- and outer-zone PFs (182 ± 2.6 nm, n = 703 vs. 159 ± 2.0 nm, n = 819 vs. 145 ± 1.7 nm, n = 1024 Figure 6A–C; PKruskal-Wallis <0.0001), which is in agreement with previous investigations reported in cat (Eccles et al., 1967), monkey (Fox and Barnard, 1957), rat (Pichitpornchai et al., 1994), and mouse (Wyatt et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inner-zone PFs have significantly higher conduction velocity (0.334 ± 0.003 m*s−1) compared with outer-zone PFs (0.287 ± 0.007 m*s−1).
source: We detected a significantly higher velocity in inner-zone PFs compared with middle- or outer-zone PFs (0.334 ± 0.003 m*s−1, n = 8 vs. 0.303 ± 0.004 m*s−1, n = 6 vs. 0.287 ± 0.007 m*s−1, n = 8; Figure 6F; PKruskal-Wallis <0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements with statistical significance testing.

claim: The absolute velocity and the gradient in the velocity from inner- to outer-zone PFs agree well with previous studies.
source: The absolute velocity and the gradient in the velocity from inner- to outer-zone PFs agree well with previous studies (Baginskas et al., 2009; Vranesic et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inner-zone PFs are specialized for fast signaling.
source: These results suggest that inner-zone PFs are specialized for fast signaling, which is consistent with the concept that inner-zone GCs are tuned for high-frequency inputs (cf. Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the conduction velocity data.

claim: Stimulation of inner-zone PFs resulted in EPSPs with shorter rise times compared with EPSPs obtained from stimulating outer-zone PFs.
source: Stimulation of inner-zone PFs resulted in EPSPs (Barbour, 1993; Roth and Häusser, 2001) with shorter rise and decay times compared with EPSPs obtained from stimulating outer-zone PFs (rise20-80: inner: 0.57 ± 0.04 ms, n = 12; middle: 0.93 ± 0.17 ms, n = 4; outer: 1.83 ± 0.33 ms, n = 12; PKruskal-Wallis = 0.0001; decay: inner: 21.9 ± 1.5 ms, middle: 39.7 ± 1.1 ms outer: 40.8 ± 4.1 ms; PKruskal-Wallis = 0.0004, Figure 7C; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements with statistical significance testing.

claim: Stimulation of inner-zone PFs resulted in EPSPs with shorter decay times compared with EPSPs obtained from stimulating outer-zone PFs.
source: Stimulation of inner-zone PFs resulted in EPSPs (Barbour, 1993; Roth and Häusser, 2001) with shorter rise and decay times compared with EPSPs obtained from stimulating outer-zone PFs (rise20-80: inner: 0.57 ± 0.04 ms, n = 12; middle: 0.93 ± 0.17 ms, n = 4; outer: 1.83 ± 0.33 ms, n = 12; PKruskal-Wallis = 0.0001; decay: inner: 21.9 ± 1.5 ms, middle: 39.7 ± 1.1 ms outer: 40.8 ± 4.1 ms; PKruskal-Wallis = 0.0004, Figure 7C; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements with statistical significance testing.

claim: Inner-zone PF inputs undergo less dendritic filtering in PCs compared with outer-zone PF inputs.
source: These results suggest that inner-zone PF inputs undergo less dendritic filtering in PCs compared with outer-zone PF inputs (De Schutter and Bower, 1994a; Roth and Häusser, 2001 but see De Schutter and Bower, 1994b).
evidence: This is an inference based on the EPSP kinetics data and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Individual EPSPs evoked from inner-zone PFs showed clear individual rising phases and peaks between each stimulus and less summation compared with outer-zone PFs.
source: Individual EPSPs evoked from inner-zone PFs showed clear individual rising phases and peaks between each stimulus and less summation compared with outer-zone PFs (Figure 7D–F; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D–F.

claim: Inner-zone PFs can transmit timing information more faithfully compared with outer-zone PFs.
source: These results suggest that inner-zone PFs can transmit timing information more faithfully compared with outer-zone PFs and thus control spike timing of PCs more precisely.
evidence: This is an inference based on the EPSP summation data.

claim: Inner-zone PFs control spike timing of PCs more precisely than outer-zone PFs.
source: These results suggest that inner-zone PFs can transmit timing information more faithfully compared with outer-zone PFs and thus control spike timing of PCs more precisely.
evidence: This is an inference based on the EPSP summation data.

claim: To obtain the spiking precision of the model containing 400 GCs with all gradients, the model without gradients required 800 GCs.
source: For example, to obtain the spiking precision of the model containing 400 GCs with all gradients, the model without gradients required 800 GCs (cf. red arrows in Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 8C.

claim: For a cerebellum exploiting gradients, the number of GCs can at least be halved while obtaining a certain temporal precision compared with a cerebellum containing no gradients.
source: This indicates that for a cerebellum exploiting gradients, the number of GCs can at least be halved while obtaining a certain temporal precision compared with a cerebellum containing no gradients.
evidence: This is an inference based on the computational modeling results.

claim: The average relative differences between the models across all sizes of the GC populations suggest an almost additive behavior of the individual gradients to the overall performance.
source: The average relative differences between the models across all sizes of the GC populations suggest an almost additive behavior of the individual gradients to the overall performance (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the computational modeling results shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The network benefits from intermixed gradients, but maximum optimization can only be obtained with correct connectivity.
source: The network benefits from these intermixed gradients, but maximum optimization can only be obtained with correct connectivity (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The impact of the gradients increased with increasing time constant of the van Rossum error calculation.
source: The impact of the gradients increased with increasing time constant (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B), indicating that rate coded signaling especially benefits from the here described gradients.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Rate coded signaling especially benefits from the described gradients.
source: The impact of the gradients increased with increasing time constant (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B), indicating that rate coded signaling especially benefits from the here described gradients.
evidence: This is an inference based on the computational modeling results.

claim: Models with all gradients showed on average about 30% faster 'frequency-switching' than models without any gradients.
source: The transition time (tT; see Materials and methods) from these fits showed that models with all gradients showed on average about 30% faster 'frequency-switching' than models without any gradients (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C–F.

claim: The experimentally determined gradients improve the spiking precision of the cerebellar cortex.
source: Thus, our modeling results show that the experimentally determined gradients improve the spiking precision, accelerate 'frequency-switching', and increase the storing capacity of the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 8.

claim: The experimentally determined gradients accelerate 'frequency-switching' in the cerebellar cortex.
source: Thus, our modeling results show that the experimentally determined gradients improve the spiking precision, accelerate 'frequency-switching', and increase the storing capacity of the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 8.

claim: The experimentally determined gradients increase the storing capacity of the cerebellar cortex.
source: Thus, our modeling results show that the experimentally determined gradients improve the spiking precision, accelerate 'frequency-switching', and increase the storing capacity of the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 8.

claim: The separation of a signal into its frequency components resembles a Fourier transformation.
source: The separation of a signal into its frequency components resembles a Fourier transformation (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and the definition of Fourier transformation.

claim: The entire GC layer with several MFs sending various frequencies to numerous GCs can execute a Fourier-like transformation.
source: Yet, our data indicate that the entire GC layer with several MFs sending various frequencies to numerous GCs can execute a Fourier-like transformation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing frequency-dependent responses.

claim: In the molecular layer, the high-frequency components of the MF signal are sent via rapidly conducting axons to proximal parts of the PC dendritic tree.
source: Indeed, in the molecular layer, the high-frequency components of the MF signal are sent via rapidly conducting axons to proximal parts of the PC dendritic tree.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data on axon conduction velocity and PF positioning.

claim: Fast (phasic) signals have a strong and rapid impact on PC firing.
source: This allows fast (phasic) signals to have a strong and rapid impact on PC firing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the EPSP kinetics data.

claim: Low-frequency components of the MF signal are conducted more slowly and elicit slower EPSPs.
source: On the other hand, low-frequency components of the MF signal are conducted more slowly and elicit slower EPSPs, allowing slow (tonic) signals to have a modulatory impact on PC firing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data on axon conduction velocity and EPSP kinetics.

claim: Slow (tonic) signals have a modulatory impact on PC firing.
source: On the other hand, low-frequency components of the MF signal are conducted more slowly and elicit slower EPSPs, allowing slow (tonic) signals to have a modulatory impact on PC firing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the EPSP kinetics data.

claim: The combination of a Fourier-like transformation in the GC layer and specialized downstream signaling pathways in the molecular layer dramatically reduce the number of required GCs for precise PC spiking.
source: Our data indicate that, in analogy to the increased storing capacity of digital audio and image compression (Jayant et al., 1993; Wallace, 1992), the combination of a Fourier-like transformation in the GC layer and specialized downstream signaling pathways in the molecular layer dramatically reduce the number of required GCs for precise PC spiking (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 8.

claim: There are at least two axes of heterogeneity in the cerebellar cortex.
source: There are at least two axes of heterogeneity in the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is a statement introducing the discussion of known heterogeneity axes.

claim: Zebrin stripes can be observed as parasagittal zones ('medio-lateral' axis) in cerebellar cortex.
source: First, Zebrin stripes can be observed as parasagittal zones ('medio-lateral' axis) in cerebellar cortex (Apps et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Firing rate, firing regularity, synaptic connectivity and synaptic plasticity differ between PCs in zebrin positive and negative zones.
source: Firing rate, firing regularity, synaptic connectivity and synaptic plasticity seems to differ between PCs in zebrin positive and negative zones (Valera et al., 2016; Wadiche and Jahr, 2005; Xiao et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There is a lobular organization ('rostro-caudal' axis) in the cerebellar cortex.
source: Second, there is a lobular organization ('rostro-caudal' axis) as shown here by the functional differences between lobules V and IX (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: GCs in lobule IX are tuned to lower frequencies than GCs in lobule V.
source: GCs in lobule IX are tuned to lower frequencies than GCs in lobule V.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The anterior cerebellum processes high-frequency or bursting signals.
source: These findings are largely in line with previous investigations (Heath et al., 2014; Witter and De Zeeuw, 2015a; Zhou et al., 2014), where the anterior cerebellum was identified to process high-frequency or bursting signals, while the vestibulo-cerebellum mainly processed lower frequency or slowly-modulating inputs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The vestibulo-cerebellum mainly processes lower frequency or slowly-modulating inputs.
source: These findings are largely in line with previous investigations (Heath et al., 2014; Witter and De Zeeuw, 2015a; Zhou et al., 2014), where the anterior cerebellum was identified to process high-frequency or bursting signals, while the vestibulo-cerebellum mainly processed lower frequency or slowly-modulating inputs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The optimal time intervals for introduction of spike timing dependent plasticity differ between the vermis and the flocculus.
source: Furthermore, the optimal time intervals for introduction of spike timing dependent plasticity differ between the vermis and the flocculus (Suvrathan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The 'depth' axis causes inner-zone GCs to be tuned to higher frequencies than outer-zone GCs.
source: In addition to these two known axes of heterogeneity, we described an axis that is orthogonal to the surface of the cerebellar cortex. This 'depth' axis causes inner-zone GCs to be tuned to higher frequencies than outer-zone GCs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1-4.

claim: Nucleo-cortical MFs and PC specifically target GCs close to the PC layer.
source: The frequency gradients along the 'depth'-axes are in line with recently described connections of nucleo-cortical MFs and PC, which specifically target GCs close to the PC layer (Gao et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Nucleo-cortical connections send slow feedback signals to the outer-zone GCs.
source: These connections send slow feedback signals to the outer-zone GCs, which –– according to our framework –– are ideally suited to process such slow modulatory signals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature and the experimental data from this study.

claim: MFs exhibit heterogeneity.
source: Independent of these specialized feedback pathways, MFs exhibit heterogeneity (Chabrol et al., 2015; Bengtsson and Jörntell, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: MFs have rosettes throughout the depth of the granule cell layer.
source: Consistent with MFs having rosettes throughout the depth of the granule cell layer (Krieger et al., 1985; Palay and Chan-Palay, 1974), our data indicate that each type of the heterogeneous MF inputs is split into its frequency components along the depth axis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Each type of the heterogeneous MF inputs is split into its frequency components along the depth axis.
source: Consistent with MFs having rosettes throughout the depth of the granule cell layer (Krieger et al., 1985; Palay and Chan-Palay, 1974), our data indicate that each type of the heterogeneous MF inputs is split into its frequency components along the depth axis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and cited literature.

claim: Superficial GCs would preferentially convey low-frequency signals to PCs.
source: Our results predict that superficial GCs, such as the ones imaged recently in the investigation of eye-blink conditioning and reward representation in the cerebellar cortex (Giovannucci et al., 2017; Wagner et al., 2017), would preferentially convey low-frequency signals to PCs and might not be representative for the full range of frequencies present over the depth of the GC layer.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the experimental data from this study.

claim: Superficial GCs might not be representative for the full range of frequencies present over the depth of the GC layer.
source: Our results predict that superficial GCs, such as the ones imaged recently in the investigation of eye-blink conditioning and reward representation in the cerebellar cortex (Giovannucci et al., 2017; Wagner et al., 2017), would preferentially convey low-frequency signals to PCs and might not be representative for the full range of frequencies present over the depth of the GC layer.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the experimental data from this study.

claim: Neurons in the medial vestibular nucleus exhibit a graded tuning of the capacity for fast-spiking by expression levels of specific ion channels.
source: Due to a large variability within each zone, our data cannot rule out a salt and pepper distribution of two populations of neurons (Espinosa and Luo, 2008). However, neurons in the medial vestibular nucleus exhibit a graded tuning of the capacity for fast-spiking by expression levels of specific ion channels (Kodama et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: There are three orthogonal axes along which the cerebellar cortex is tuned for preferred frequency.
source: Thus, including this new 'depth' axis, there are three orthogonal axes along which the cerebellar cortex is tuned for preferred frequency, indicating the importance of proper frequency tuning of the circuitry.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and prior literature.

claim: The dendrites of basket cells are preferentially located at the inner-zone of the molecular layer.
source: Although the dendrites of molecular layer interneurons can span the entire molecular layer, the dendrites of basket cells seem to be preferentially located at the inner-zone of the molecular layer (Palkovits et al., 1971; Rakic, 1972), which positions them ideally to receive rapid high-frequency signals of inner-zone PFs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Basket cells impact PC firing rapidly and efficiently via their pinceaus.
source: Consistently, they impact PC firing rapidly and efficiently via their pinceaus (Blot and Barbour, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The dendrites of a subset of stellate cells are preferentially located at the outer-zone molecular layer.
source: Furthermore, the dendrites of a subset of stellate cells (with their somata located in the outer-zone molecular layer) are preferentially located at the outer-zone molecular layer (Palkovits et al., 1971; Rakic, 1972), which positions them ideally to receive modulatory low-frequency signals and elicit slow IPSPs in PCs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Molecular layer interneurons represent a continuum along the vertical axis.
source: Furthermore, molecular layer interneurons seem to represent a continuum along the vertical axis, with a correlation between the vertical location of the soma, axonal boutons, and dendrite location (Sultan and Bower, 1998), which is consistent with the here-described continuum of biophysical properties along the vertical axis of the cortex.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: MF firing frequencies range from <1 to ~1000 Hz.
source: MF firing frequencies range from <1 to ~1000 Hz (Arenz et al., 2008; Chadderton et al., 2004; Jörntell and Ekerot, 2006; Rancz et al., 2007; van Kan et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Many previous modeling studies investigating cerebellar function considered the activity of each MF as a constant digital value.
source: Many previous modeling studies investigating cerebellar function considered the activity of each MF as a constant digital value (Albus, 1971; Babadi and Sompolinsky, 2014; Brunel et al., 2004; Clopath et al., 2012; Marr, 1969), a constant analog value (Chabrol et al., 2015; Clopath and Brunel, 2013), or spike sequences with constant frequency (Billings et al., 2014; Cayco-Gajic et al., 2017; Steuber et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PC firing rate and spiking precision have been shown to be closely related to movement.
source: PC firing rate and spiking precision have been shown to be closely related to movement (Brown and Raman, 2018; Sarnaik and Raman, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A significant reduction in the number of GCs could represent an evolutionary advantage to minimize neuronal maintenance energy.
source: Taking into account the large number of cerebellar GCs in the brain (Herculano-Houzel, 2009; Williams and Herrup, 1988), a significant reduction in the number of GCs could represent an evolutionary advantage to minimize neuronal maintenance energy (Howarth et al., 2012; Isler and van Schaik, 2006).
evidence: This is speculation based on the modeling results and citations to prior literature on neuronal energy costs.

claim: The dramatic increase in storing capacity for precise PC spiking provides an evolutionary explanation for the emergence of gradients in the neuronal properties.
source: Therefore, the dramatic increase in storing capacity for precise PC spiking provides an evolutionary explanation for the emergence of gradients in the neuronal properties.
evidence: This is speculation based on the modeling results.

claim: Descending motor commands from the pyramidal tract send broadband signals to motoneurons with different input resistances resulting from differences in size.
source: To our knowledge, this has rarely been shown explicitly, but similar mechanisms might operate, for example, in the spinal cord network: descending motor commands from the pyramidal tract send broadband signals to motoneurons with different input resistances resulting from differences in size.
evidence: This is speculation about potential similar mechanisms in other neural networks.

claim: Small motoneurons fire during low-frequency inputs and large motoneurons only during high-frequency inputs.
source: This enables small motoneurons to fire during low-frequency inputs and large motoneurons only during high-frequency inputs (Henneman et al., 1965).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Specialized efferent down-stream signaling pathways innervate specific types of muscles with specialized short-term plasticity of the corresponding neuromuscular junctions.
source: Furthermore, specialized efferent down-stream signaling pathways innervate specific types of muscles with specialized short-term plasticity of the corresponding neuromuscular junctions (Wang and Brehm, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Frequency preferences of hippocampal neurons enable segregation of compound oscillatory input into distinct frequency components.
source: In the hippocampus, frequency preferences of hippocampal neurons are well established in enabling segregation of compound oscillatory input into distinct frequency components (Pike et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: CA3 pyramidal neurons exhibit gradients in intrinsic electrical properties and synaptic connectivity.
source: Furthermore, there is increasing evidence that what has been considered a homogeneous population of neurons exhibit gradients in the neuronal properties (Cembrowski and Spruston, 2019), such as the intrinsic electrical properties and synaptic connectivity in CA3 pyramidal neurons (Galliano et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Heterogeneity enables functional segregation of information streams in CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: The here reported heterogeneity furthermore enables functional segregation of information streams for example in CA1 pyramidal neurons (Soltesz and Losonczy, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Gradients in biophysical properties of neurons in the entorhinal cortex might serve to generate functional outcomes relevant for the generation of grid cell sizes.
source: Additionally, gradients in biophysical properties of neurons in the entorhinal cortex might serve to generate functional outcomes relevant for the generation of grid cell sizes (Giocomo et al., 2007; Schmidt-Hieber and Nolan, 2017; Orchard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Gradients in anatomical and biophysical properties were recently uncovered in the neocortex.
source: Finally, in the neocortex, gradients in anatomical and biophysical properties were recently uncovered (Fletcher and Williams, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Gradients facilitate complex transformation of information, such as Fourier-like transformations, to cope with a broad temporal diversity of signals in the central nervous system.
source: Our data furthermore suggest that such gradients facilitate complex transformation of information, such as Fourier-like transformations, to cope with a broad temporal diversity of signals in the central nervous system.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental and modeling data from this study.
